newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA CLONES TOBACCO, SEEKS MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA CLONES TOBACCO, SEEKS MARKETS.

text.p: Cloning sheep? Not yet. But ingenious Bulgarian scientists have used cloning techniques to develop tobacco strains that are resistant to disease, pests and environmental stress,
"We expect to be the first in Europe to have created cloned tobacco varieties that field," the director of the Institute of Genetic Engineering Atanas Atanassov told Reuters in an interview.

Agrochemical industry leaders like Philip Morris and Hoechst Schering Agrevo Ltd , have shown interest in the cloned tobacco varieties but Bulgaria's political and economic crisis has delayed further development.

After 10 years of research the institute has created transgenic virus-resistant lines for 12 varieties of tobacco, which have passed field tests and can save growers millions of dollars spent on pesticides.
Bulgaria alone, where tobacco remains a major export, spends $25 million annually on pesticides.
The new varieties are created by introducing a gene of a widespread plant virus into a tobacco plant's RNA molecule which is the carrier of hereditary information.
The plant that grows after this operation, immune to the virus, is cloned into more plants which then have the same immunity.

The cloned plants grow bigger and stronger than their original counterparts, with a better tobacco quality because their leaves are untainted by herbicides and pesticides and retain their natural flavour.

The technique, also applicable for cloning apple trees, barley and tomatoes, is environmentally harmless, said Atanassov, as it does not transform protein contained in the major hereditory information carrier, the DNA molecule.

The sponsor of the research, state tobacco monopolist Bulgartabac, has suffered like other local institutions from frequent cabinet changes and has delayed a decision on the future of the cloned tobacco, though the breakthrough could bring in some desperately needed cash.

Bulgarian tobacco exports fell to about 15,000 tonnes in 1995, from 50,000 tonnes in better years. The buyers are mainly western companies like Philip Morris, Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp, French tobacco group Seita and B.A.T Industries Plc .
Scientific research in Bulgaria was once generously funded as a showcase of the communist regime, but seven years of economic mismanagement have reduced it to misery.
The caretaker government in power until parliamentary elections on April 19, is struggling to win foreign funding to pay billion-dollar foreign debts and secure vital imports like grain and fuel.
But Atanassov, whose numerous projects thrive mostly on western resarch funding programmes, is optimistic.
"Modern farming and biotechnology are inseparable and Bulgaria will one day come to terms with this," he said.
